name: Chives
summary: Mild onion-flavored leaves and pretty purple flowers. A no-fuss perennial for a pot or a border.
problems: Very few. Clumps get crowded after a few years; dig and divide them in spring.
greenhouse_notes: A pot brought into a cool greenhouse gives fresh leaves most of the winter.
notes: Buying a pot or getting a division from a friend is quicker than seed. The flowers are edible.

name: Thyme
summary: A small, woody herb for soups, beans and roasts. Loves sun and dry soil, and lives for years.
problems: Rots in wet or heavy soil. Plants get woody and sparse after three or four years; start new ones from cuttings.
notes: Seed is tiny and slow, so most people buy a plant. Cut stems just before it flowers and dry them in bundles.

name: Rosemary
summary: A fragrant evergreen shrub for meats, bread and potatoes. Thrives on heat, sun and neglect.
problems: Overwatering kills more rosemary than cold does. Powdery mildew indoors in still air.
greenhouse_notes: In cold places a pot spends winter in a cool, bright greenhouse or window.
notes: Start with a plant or a cutting; seed is slow and unreliable. Some kinds handle colder winters than others, so ask the nursery.

name: Mint
summary: Fast, fragrant leaves for tea, drinks and salads. It spreads everywhere, so it is happiest in its own pot.
problems: Runners take over a bed in a season. Rust spots the leaves in humid weather; cut it back hard and it regrows.
notes: Plant a rooted piece or a pot; mint grown from seed is often not true to type. Sink a bottomless pot into the ground to hold it in. Goats love it.

name: Sage
summary: Soft gray leaves for stuffing, beans and sausage. A sturdy perennial that likes it dry.
problems: Rots in wet soil and humid summers. Woody after four or five years.
notes: Pick lightly the first year. Cut the plant back by a third in spring to keep it bushy, and dry leaves flat on a screen.

name: Epazote
summary: A strong, resinous herb cooked with black beans in Mexican kitchens. Grows easily, even in poor soil.
problems: Reseeds heavily and can become weedy. Cut the seed heads off before they ripen.
notes: Use only a sprig or a few leaves per pot of beans. It is a strong herb, and eating large amounts is not safe, so keep it a seasoning and keep the plants away from grazing animals. Avoid it during pregnancy.

name: Lemongrass
summary: A tall tropical grass with a lemony base for soups, curries and tea. Grows fast in heat.
problems: Any frost damages it. Leaf edges are sharp; wear gloves when you cut.
greenhouse_notes: In cold places, pot it up before frost and keep it in a bright, frost-free spot over winter.
notes: Fresh stalks from the grocery store root in a glass of water in two or three weeks, then go in a pot.
